text: It's tempting to jump straight to a fact model and start writing joins. The Beginner project already proved why that's the wrong order: staging models keep cleanup logic in one place per source, and marts models keep business logic downstream of anything source-specific. Plan the layer first.

Beyond raw_customers, this chapter needs two more real jaffle shop seed tables. raw_orders: one row per order, with id, user_id, order_date, and status. raw_payments: one row per payment, with id, order_id, payment_method, and amount — in cents, a real detail that comes back in Lesson 7.

The planned layer, top to bottom: staging models, one per raw source, same pattern as the Beginner project's customers staging model. An intermediate model that joins the orders staging model to the already-built customers mart. And a marts model — the orders fact table Finance and Ops will both query.

A staging model's only job is cleaning up one source. The moment you join to a different source — the customers mart — that's combining business entities, which is exactly what an intermediate model is for. Keeping that join out of staging keeps the orders staging model simple and reusable.
Next lesson: building the orders staging model — stg_jaffle_shop__orders.sql, straight from raw_orders.
